catalog_locator: Arnold 2026, sec. 3.1 'Phonology', p. 28 (journal pagination), paragraph beginning 'Unlike Maˈya'; supporting gloss p. 27 (realisations of /q/); tone pp. 29-30. Corroboration: Arnold 2025 ms sec. 5.1 and Table 25 (ms p. 36) and ms p. 41.
catalog_quote: [p. 28] Unlike Maˈya, there is no contrastive lexical stress in Batta; with a handful of exceptions, stress is predictably word‑final. As introduced above, a large proportion of the polysyllabic lexicon of Batta (approximately two thirds) can be analysed as sesquisyllabic, in that the nucleus of non‑final syllables is an underspecified vowel (represented here as /ə/), the realisation of which is determined by a combination of the vowel of the final syllable and the surrounding consonants. [p. 27] The realisation of /q/ is very variable, both within and between speakers. In the onset of stressed (i.e., word-final) syllables, possible realisations of /q/ are [q], fricative [χ], or pharyngeal stop [ʡ]; in the onset of unstressed (i.e., non-final) syllables, /q/ may be realised as [q], [χ], or [ʡ], or be deleted ... [p. 1, abstract] Batta has 15 consonants, 6 vowels, tone, and no contrastive stress but a largely sesquisyllabic profile. [Arnold 2025 ms p. 36] Batta, like Northern Salawati, does not have contrastive stress ... [ms p. 41] today all Salawati‑Batta varieties have predictable final stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Batta is not contrastive and falls predictably on the word-final syllable (which is also the only syllable that may carry one of the three lexical tones High/Rise/Low); non-final syllables are unstressed and mostly have a reduced/underspecified vowel (sesquisyllabic words).
new_statements.exceptions: 'with a handful of exceptions' (not itemised in the sketch). Toneless words optionally take a prepausal epenthetic /-o/; the sketch does not say whether this epenthetic syllable affects stress. Arnold 2025 (OL, accepted ms p. 41) corroborates: 'today all Salawati-Batta varieties have predictable final stress'; ms p. 36 and Table 25: Batta has no contrastive stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (lexical/phonological word incl. subject prefixes); based on survey data (429-item list plus elicitation, 2019 and 2023, Yenenas village). Batta is a tone language (High, Rise, Low vs toneless, culminative but not obligatory, restricted to the final syllable) with an explicit stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the language 'Batta' (Glottolog bata1295 'Batanta', alt. name 'Batta'; Arnold's CV explicitly tags Batta as [bata1295]). Described variety: Batta of Yenenas village (also spoken in Weyman and Wailebet), south coast of Batanta island; c. 150 speakers, all born before c. 1980. Arnold treats Batta as a distinct language closely related to (possibly a divergent dialect of) the Salawati varieties (made1253), within Ma'ya-Salawati. Glottolog 5.1 still lists Batanta as undocumented/possibly extinct with zero descriptive refs; Arnold 2026 (LD&C 20) is the first published sketch and supersedes the earlier scan classification 'no source found'.

tone_statements.citation: Arnold, Laura. 2021. The tonal phonologies of three undocumented Raja Ampat languages. Talk, The P-Workshop (Phonetics/Phonology Workshop), Linguistics and English Language, University of Edinburgh, 5 March 2021 (abstract online); also presented at the 15th International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics (15-ICAL), Palacky University, Olomouc [online], 28 June-1 July 2021.
tone_statements.quote: In this talk, I will present a first look at data from the three other Raja Ampat languages – the Butlih variety of Salawati, Batta, and Biga – collected during a recent field trip (Nov 2019-Jan 2020). Using these data, I will present analyses of the phonologies of the three languages, focussing on the word-prosodic systems. I will show that Butlih Salawati, Batta, and Biga all have lexical tone, just like the better-described Raja Ampat languages.

sources.note: Footnote 2 (p. 8) reports the author's own preliminary 2015 fieldwork on Biga, Batta and As and states he 'found apparent tonal minimal pairs in all three' -- the earliest published first-hand indication that Batta has lexical tone, independent of and prior to Arnold's 2019-23 data; no tone inventory, TBU or stress statement for Batta. (Arnold 2026: 28 cites exactly this footnote: 'As first suggested in Kamholz (2016) and mentioned in Kamholz (2017: 8 f.n. 2), Batta.. has lexical tone.') Consistent with the statement listed here (3 tones per Arnold 2026), not contradicting it.
